newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Toppy Canada dollar may wound debt.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Toppy Canada dollar may wound debt.

text.p: Investors in Canadian bonds have recently witnessed the most impressive outperformance of U.S. Treasuries in more than a decade. But the fate of debt holdings now lies with the heart of currency markets.

While a rising Canadian dollar, falling interest rates, tame inflation and a solid turnaround in government finances have helped narrow Canadian/U.S. debt yield spreads, analysts on Wednesday said caution will soon be the order of the day.

"The spreads are based on a view that we have a golden scenario for the Canadian dollar, that it can appreciate further against the U.S. dollar," said Michael Burke, bond strategist at Citibank in London.
"And although I think it will, the market may be overdoing the extent of the optimism," he said.

Spreads between 30-year U.S. and Canadian bonds pinched in to 11-year lows on Tuesday, while 10-year Canadian yields were 13 basis points below their U.S. rivals on Wednesday, having been 116 basis points above just six months ago.
The Canadian dollar has risen about 2.5 percent against the U.S. dollar in the past three months. It was at C$1.3460/70 per U.S. at 1152 GMT, versus C$1.3451 at Tuesday's close.

But there may be official opposition to further Canadian dollar strength -- especially as this could undermine progress already made in turning the current account around -- and analysts say bond investors stand to gain little as a result.
Citibank's Burke said recent debt price rallies had sprung from a sharp tightening up of government finances.

"We've seen a sea change in Canadian accounts -- the current account has come from a huge deficit to a small surplus and both government and provincial deficits are on a much more even course -- and a result we have seen spreads collapse," he said.
Analysts pointed to a bucketful of bond positive fundamentals which could urge further outperformance of Canadian bonds in the near term.

"The economy has been showing fairly significant signs of weakenss, retail sales data were weak side of expectations, inflation is under control and there is further scope for the Bank of Canada to cut interest rates," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London.
"In the interim we could easily see the 10-year spread go to minus 25 or minus 30 basis points."
The Bank of Canada slashed its key bank rate by 25 basis points to 3.75 percent last week -- its lowest level in decades.

While the move was already the ninth cut this year, analysts, citing year-on-year core inflation of 1.2 percent and latest retail sales data showing a 0.4 percent fall, say there is room for more monetary easing.
But beyond a two or three month boundary, analysts said a toppy Canadian dollar would spawn risks for bond holders.
"The problem for Canada is that 85 percent of its exports go to the U.S., so significant Canadian dollar appreciation will leave the current account position vulnerable," said Burke.

Canada authorities, concerned that trade gains might be eroded, are likely to erect barriers against further currency strength at C$1.33, a level that has previously capped the Canada dollar, he said.
The Canadian 10-year yield spread could push to minus 20 basis points in the near term, but he suggested investors start to look elsewhere when this level was reached.
Dick Howard, senior economist at Julius Baer Investments in London, was also sceptical about Canadian bonds, saying the central bank's easing policy was approaching dangerous ground.

"The last two rate cuts from the BoC have been specifically on the back of a stronger Canadian dollar. What they are telling the market is "If you push the dollar up, we'll cut interest rates' -- which is giving the market a one-way bet," he said.
"And as soon as a central bank gives the market a one-way bet, it is making trouble for itself further down the line."
-- Kate Kelland, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 8682
